speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the government refuses to recognize the devastating effects on this country's voluntary groups of its proposed massive increases in postal rates. For example, the $1,200 annual increase in postal costs to the Waterloo regional branch of the Canadian Mental Health Association will make it extremely difficult for that agency to mobilize its 250 volunteers. That this House urge the minister responsible for the Canada Post Corporation, the Secretary of State in his role as minister responsible for the voluntary action program, or the Minister of Finance, to stand in his place and tell the volunteers of Canada why this government is ignoring and stifling the giving and caring spirit which are more needed than ever due to unprecedented unemployment and inflation.

All CMHC owned and operated apartments located in the lower mainland of B.C., and in many other parts of Canada, are insulated with poisonous urea formaldehyde foam. subsubtopic: PROTECTION OF POLAR BEAR PASS-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. Given the fact that the international biological program has identified the Polar Bear Pass in the Canadian Arctic as one of approximately 140 environmentally sensitive sites that are worthy of protection, and given the fact that the interdepartmental working group has recently issued a report calling for multiple land use in the Pass so as to accommodate the interests of non-renewable resource developers, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Churchill (Mr. Murphy):
That the federal government reject the recommendations being made by the working group and immediately take steps to ensure that this environmentally sensitive area will be protected from the future activities of resource developers.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance. Madam Speaker, I want to pursue the question of privilege which the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) flagged last Wednesday. It has to do, of course, with the right of the House and the members of the House to accurate answers from members of the ministry.
The nineteenth edition of Erskine May's Parliamentary Practice, at pages 141 and 142, shows very clearly that misleading the House of Commons is considered a very serious contempt of that institution, whether it is done by false documents, conspiracy to deceive or by a deliberately misleading statement. Two paragraphs in particular of that citation are of interest. The first at page 141 sets forth as follows:
It has already been seen that the giving of false evidence, prevarication or suppression of the truth by witnesses while under examination before either House or before committees of either House is punished as a contempt; and that persons who present false, forged or fabricated documents to either House or to committees of either House are guilty of a breach of privilege. Conspiracy to deceive either House or any committees of either House will also be treated as a breach of privilege.
The second paragraph on page 142 reads as follows:
The House may treat the making of a deliberately misleading statement as a contempt.
In 1963 the House resolved that in making a personal statement which contained words which he later admitted not to be true, a former Member had been guilty of a grave contempt.
That citation referred to the Profumo case with which the Chair is very familiar.
These paragraphs show very clearly in my submission, Madam Speaker, that the House has always considered that it
has the right to hear the truth, and any attempt to mislead the House is considered as a contempt and treated as such.
Our own precedents show that deliberately misleading the House can be done indirectly with a member or a minister being, in a sense, an agent of misrepresentation, but not himself culpable in contempt. That particular case was raised by the hon. member for Durham-Northumberland (Mr. Lawrence), who was then the member for Northumberland-Dur-ham, in 1978 and it is very critical here to your consideration, Madam Speaker.
Mr. Speaker Jerome said on that occasion, which involved the drafting of a deliberately misleading reply to a letter from the hon. member for Durham-Northumberland:
The complaint which is the subject matter of the question of privilege is not directly-

I would like to hear that. Of course, all these citations from Erskine May, to the effect that if someone has deliberately misled the House, or admitted that he has contradicted himself, he may be in contempt of this House, and of course that is true, relate to a description of what contempt of the House really is. speechtext:
So as to get on with the matter, Madam Speaker, I will set aside the linkage which 1 intend to submit to the Chair but the argument and the presentation is now disrupted. I presented May's, I will set aside the argument with respect to our own precedents and I will now lay the facts out for the Chair and, I hope, for the minister.
It is my submission, Madam Speaker, that in the case at hand involving the minister responsible for housing, the House has clearly been misled. The question that it outstanding is, by whom?
Now, had I been allowed to present the precedent in our Canadian House, that question would be more relevant, but I will have to come back to it when I am through giving my version of the facts. I will suggest that both possible answers to the question "By whom?" lead us irrevocably to the conclusion that a contempt has occurred, thereby justifying an investigation by the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections.
According to the citation from May and the citations which I have yet to make, the issue of a possible leak was first raised

December 11, 1981
Privilege-Mr. Lewis
in the House on Tuesday, November 17, as reported in Hansard at page 12827.	.
When asked about this suspiciously early appearance of budget advertisements, the minister said this:
-I learned generally of the provisions of the budget as they pertain to housing at a briefing of the cabinet by the Minister of Finance on Thursday afternoon. I learned specifically and saw the budget documents a few minutes before they were presented by the Minister of Finance in the House. My officials worked from five o'clock in the afternoon, through the evening, and early the next morning, and produced for my inspection that document-
Referring to the advertisement.
-which had been worked upon. It was authorized at noon on November 13 as a result of a meeting of the communications cabinet of the Government of Canada, as I say on Friday, November 13.
The minister clearly denied any early knowledge or early communication to anyone not properly involved in the budget process. In fact, he said that neither he nor his officials knew what was in the budget.
Not surprisingly, Madam Speaker, the issue was raised again by the hon. member for Leeds-Grenville (Mr. Cossitt) on Wednesday, November 18, when the minister had obviously had a chance to talk to his officials and make sure that he was giving the story not only as he knew it but as they knew it. The minister added to his story but did not change any material particular. At page 12886 of Hansard, the minister said:
-I have had the opportunity since responding to the questions yesterday afternoon to speak to officials on this matter. I would confirm that the story reported in The Globe and Mail today, on page 8, does consist of the facts as I understand them. The facts are correct that, first, no publication of any material affecting housing in the budget was printed until after the budget, that is, November 13.
Said the minister:
I also confirm that no material pertaining to that advertisement was in the hands of the firm to which the hon. gentleman has just referred. Indeed, their work for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation was to obtain space, which they did.
I would add, finally, that after the budget was delivered in this House, representatives of Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation released an advertisement, which was then taken to the newspapers after the budget was delivered-
The minister, therefore, has given a statement to the House before and after consultation with his officials that no one outside the normal and accepted process had access to budget material. On occasion, the minister even implied that it was just dumb luck that the final advertisement had the exact text of the budgetary proposal.
The question was again pursued on Tuesday, December 3, when the hon. member for Leeds-Grenville had investigated further. In response to that question the minister said, as reported at page 13683:
-the brief answer is that no person was aware who was not authorized and under normal budgetary security-all employees or civil servants in the employ or control of the federal government, no person beyond those was aware or had in their possession the particulars of the ad-
The hon. member then asked a supplementary question and even repeated the reference to Studio S & B which was mentioned by the hon. member for Leeds-Grenville. The minister repeated his story and again I quote from page 13684:
-I will stand by my previous answer today and on other occasions in this House. I would say to the hon. gentleman that the employee he is referring to, Mr. Crombie, was in a lockup prior to the budget and he was there until the normal time when the media and all authorized people in that lockup were released.
The next day, Madam Speaker, a new truth appeared and the story changed. The minister now said, as I quote from page 13728 of Hansard:
The Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation officials had charge of the security of this document until such time as it was delivered to the newspapers after the speech. They were assisted by some employees of the firm of S & B in Montreal.
They were assisted by typesetters who assisted in setting up the document. It was prepared by CMHC in anticipation that the recommendations to the Minister of Finance by me would be accepted and would be in the budget as announced. When that was confirmed, Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation authorized the release of those documents which were in sealed envelopes-
Madam Speaker, the House clearly had been misled and upon reflecting on how that occurred, the House has two clear and unavoidable alternatives. They are, either the minister deliberately misled the House and finally gave in and told the truth when he had no alternative but to do so, and in doing so admitted that his earlier statements were false, or the minister's officials misled the minister, causing him to mislead the House and those officials did not give up and tell him the truth until they had no choice.
The first alternative is a contempt under the Profumo citation, which is already submitted and is on the record, and the second is a contempt which is a prima facie case of privilege under the specific terms of the ruling to which I might now refer, now that this degree of fact is before the Chair.
The ruling of Mr. Speaker Jerome on the case of the second alternative, the one that was raised by the hon. member for Northumberland-Durham, as his constituency was then called, was:
The complaint which is the subject matter of the question of privilege is not directly a complaint about the minister. Indeed, it is founded on the fact that it is one of the minister's officials who has calculated to contrive this deliberate deception of the House. In fact I have indicated some concern about the fact that this may perhaps be looked upon as a new departure in our practice-that we are going around the minister to get directly at the official by way of this question of privilege. Even if that is so, I have come to the conclusion that it is not a procedural basis upon which I can intervene. Once again, it is a matter to which the House can address itself in debate, and in amendment if necessary, or in a vote-
On that occasion Mr. Speaker Jerome went on to say:
That leaves us with the complaint of the hon. member for Northumberland-Durham respecting the testimony of former commissioner Higgitt-and I assume there is no further argument to be addressed to this matter at this time- to the circumstances in which the Solicitor General's letter dated September 4, 1973, was drafted. Does that lead us to the conclusion that, by virtue of an act or ommission, the House, or a member, has directly or indirectly been impeded in the performance of its functions or his duty, or that there has been a tendency to produce such result? If I so find, then I really have no choice but to find, prima facie, that a contempt has been committed.
The Speaker then quoted from the commissioner's testimony that letters were not drafted "on precise statements of fact". Mr. Speaker Jerome concluded in this fashion:
December 11, 1981

I can interpret that testimony in no other way than meaning that a deliberate attempt was made to obstruct the member in the performance of his duties, and consequently, to obstruct the House itself.
Even beyond the precedents and the complex law of privilege, I cannot conceive that there is any one of us who would accept the argument that this House of Commons has no recourse in the face of such an attempt to obstruct by offering admittedly misleading information.
This citation has two key points. First, the House does have a right not to be deliberately misled and, second, the ruling established that a contempt has occurred if an official misleads a minister and causes him to mislead the House. That was the argument I wanted up front to support the two alternatives I put to the Chair. I submit at this stage that the Chair now sees the logic of that form of presentation.
In conclusion, I suggest that since a reference to a committee is required either way-the Chair can adopt either option-the House should be allowed to make a decision on a reference, and it can only be allowed to do that, of course, if the Chair finds that prima facie there is a case of privilege. I hope no one in the House will suggest that, because we are not sure which of the citations applies, neither should, because such a result would be rather absurd. A contempt has unquestionably, in my submission, been committed according to both logic and precedent in both instances.
If you find that there is a prima facie question of privilege, this is the form of motion I would move:
That this House, having been misled by the answers of the minister responsible for housing, either directly by the misinformation admittedly supplied to the House by the minister responsible for housing, or by officials of the minister, who in misleading the minister misled the House, declares that a contempt of this House has occurred, and refers the question to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections for investigation and report.
Finally, I strongly suggest, in view of the very serious nature of this matter in terms of the consequences your ruling on it will have on this particular privilege of the House and its members, that you follow the very excellent course of your predecessor, Mr. Speaker Jerome, when he had under consideration the question of privilege raised by the hon. member for Northumberland-Durham, as he then was, take the matter under consideration until you have very carefully reviewed the precedents I have cited and provide us with a ruling after you have had that full opportunity to give this matter the careful review and consideration it deserves, having regard to the very serious downstream consequences it could have on the privileges of all of us and of this institution.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I will be quite brief. In response to the minister's intervention, I would say that what the minister suggested was totally irrelevant to the issue that is before the Chair at the present time. The issue is not whether it is inconvenient or difficult for the minister to maintain a balance between consultation with industry and the question of the need for budget secrecy. The issue which the Chair is asked to adjudicate upon is whether the House was misled and whether such misleading of the House constitutes a breach of the privileges of Members of Parliament.
I want to underline two very relevant portions from Hansard which make it very clear to me that the House was given false information. I bring first to your attention page 12827 of Hansard of November 17, 1981, where the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Cosgrove) said the following:
Madam Speaker, I learned generally of the provisions of the budget as they pertain to housing at a briefing of the cabinet by the Minister of Finance on Thursday afternoon. I learned specifically and saw the budget documents a few minutes before they were presented by the Minister of Finance in the House. My officials worked from five o'clock in the afternoon, through the evening, and early the next morning, and produced for my inspection that document which had been worked upon. It was authorized at noon on November 13 as a result of a meeting of the communications cabinet of the Government of Canada, as I say on Friday, November 13.
The document that was referred to when the hon. member for Leeds-Grenville (Mr. Cossitt) put the question to the minister was that ad which appeared over the minister's signature and which was placed by CMHC.
The minister has since conceded to the House that the truth was that the ad was prepared well in advance and that indeed it was distributed to various distribution points in Canada prior to the time that was mentioned by the minister in the House or his officials working over the document from five o'clock in the afternoon, into the evening until early the next morning. In fact, the advertisement had been prepared well in advance. The information had been communicated to the officials of Studio S & B some days in advance and very clearly the statement made by the minister at page 12827 simply does not bear any relationship to the facts.
Second, when the minister was questioned by various members in the House, he tried to give some indication as to when he was first informed and when his officials were first informed. At page 12834 of Hansard, the minister was asked by my colleague, the hon. member for Saskatoon West (Mr. Hnatyshyn) about the time the information was conveyed to various officials. He said the following:
Madam Speaker, the hon. member indicated as he rose to ask the question that he would be repeating a question. I will repeat my answer. I was not aware of the provisions in the budget pertaining to housing until the Minister of Finance released in this House, or almost simultaneous with that.

speechtext:
Nor was the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation knowledgeable as to what was in the budget, nor were they authorized to release or request publication of any advertisement that had to deal with the budget prior to that time.
What we have now learned is that in fact officials from CMHC had had confirmation that these provisions would be in the budget. They asked that the ads be prepared. The ads were indeed prepared and sent to various distribution points in the country for distribution once the budget was brought down.
Those ads were sent out. They were prepared on the basis of this information prior to the budget being brought down. That is why the Chair must look very carefully at the statements that were made on the record by the minister. Any sensible reading of the statements that were made simply leave us in a situation where it is impossible to reconcile what the minister said with the facts which we all know to be true at this time, and the facts which were conceded by the minister at a later date and were conceded, incidentally, by his officials.
Mr. Crombie himself has in fact confirmed publicly, and other officials from CMHC have, that those ads were worked upon in advance and that the information was prepared in advance and distributed in advance. It left the control of the officers of the government later in the evening once the budget was brought down, but the ads had been prepared and sent to various distribution points in the country prior to the release of the budget.
It is impossible to reconcile what the minister says with the truth and to find that in fact he was reporting on a factual basis to the House. Consequently that is the issue which the Chair is being asked to rule on; it is not the issue of whether or not it was difficult for the minister to balance budget secrecy with the need for consultation with private industry, but the question of whether or not the information given by the minister to the House was truthful and factual and whether on the face of it there is sufficient evidence to merit study by a committee.

speakeroldname: Mr. David Smith (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: MR. LEWIS-FAILURE BY MR. COSGROVE TO CLARIFY ALLEGED CONTRADICTORY STATEMENTS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the arguments made by the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) are almost entirely based on the item found in Erskine May, nineteenth edition, page 142 where it refers to the misconduct of members or officers of either House as such deliberately misleading the House. It states:
The House may treat the making of a deliberately misleading statement as a contempt.
Prior to the Profumo case, I do not believe that there had been a reference to such a matter as constituting what might be analogous to a question of privilege, as whether a contempt is the same as a question of privilege, is arguable. I do not believe that was in there prior to that.
I do not think the situation we are talking about here has anything to do with the type of facts that were found in the Profumo case. In the Profumo case, a minister stood in the House and admitted to the House that he had lied. If we look at the citations we have in Canada as to whether this constitutes a question of privilege, the clearest point is found on page 12 of Beauchesne, Section 19(1), and I quote:
December 11, 1981

A dispute arising between two Members, as to allegation of facts, does not fulfil the conditions of parliamentary privilege.
This is really what we have here, a dispute between members as to the allegation of facts. In the opinion of some people there are contradictory statements. That is a dispute. We have not had a minister stand up and say that he has deliberately misled the House. I do not think there is any suggestion of that.
When the matter was first raised by the hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Lewis) the other day, he invited the Chair to break new ground and to extend the bounds of parliamentary privilege. I refer Your Honour to page 40 of the fourth edition of Bourinot where it is stated:
Each house, however, exercises and vindicates its own privileges independently of the other. At the same time it has been established by the highest authorities that although either house may expound the law of Parliament and vindicate its own privileges, it is agreed that no new privilege can be created.
Your Honour has been invited to create a new ground of privilege. It is suggested that somehow the area that really is, in my view, debate, a dispute over what the facts are, cannot be drawn into the ambit of the one reference in Erskine May which talks about deliberately misleading the House. This matter was covered very well by Speaker Michener in a ruling which appears in the Journals of the House of Commons of June 17, 1959, and was again referred to on October 30, 1964. I quote the words of Speaker Michener:
In my view, simple justice requires that no honourable Member should have to submit to investigation of his conduct by the House or a Committee until he has been charged with an offence.
What is an offence? Are contradictory statements an offence? It has been alleged that the statements are contradictory. In my opinion, that is a matter of dispute. Even if it was agreed, and it is not, that there had been contradictory statements, that does not constitute an offence. We do not have an offence. I do not think we have a charge. The Speaker on the same occasion, and this is at page 11268, repeated:
Once more there is nothing to prevent the hon. member from bringing a charge, properly drafted.
I would also refer the Chair to Hansard of October 30, 1964, at page 9595. I believe this was a statement made by Speaker Macnaughton. He stated:
It is undoubtedly a very serious thing to attack the conduct of any member of the House of Commons, and in that respect a specific charge should always be made, not a general charge. I am confirmed in this opinion by an excellent ruling ... given by Mr. Speaker Michener on June 19, 1959-
That is the ruling I have just referred to.
The other day when the hon. member for the Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) wanted to reserve the right of raising this matter as a question of privilege, he referred to an incident when Mr. Pearson was Prime Minister. I looked up what l believed was the ruling to which the hon. member referred. In that ruling the words of Speaker Michener that I have just cited were reiterated.
Journals of the House of Commons for December 17, 1964, at page 1012, gives the ruling as follows:
Privilege-Mr. Lewis
Here we are dealing with a misstatement, not a question of privilege. There must be a real accusation made against-in this case-the Right Honourable the Prime Minister, and there must be something in the charge which shows the misstatement, if it was a misstatement, was made with intent, with purpose. There is no specific charge and in view of the ruling of Speaker Michener and of what I have said, in my opinion there is not a prima facie case and therefore no question of privilege.
The one precedent that the hon. member for Yukon raised the other day, we have not heard too much about today, and after having an opportunity to read it, I understand why we did not hear too much about it.
I should also like to refer to some comments made by the late Right Hon. John Diefenbaker. This is found on page 4825 of Hansard of June 17, 1959. Approximately two weeks ago we were having a dispute about whether or not a budget leak had occurred. There were certain innuendoes made that the minister had been responsible for a budget leak. In referring to the action that was taken by Mr. Porter, who made the charge at that time, Mr. Diefenbaker said at page 4826 of Hansard of June 17, 1959:
He went into detail and finally moved the motion, which is found at page 2405. He took the course-not the course of innuendo, insinuation and inference-that members have taken in every generation in this parliament. He made a charge, and this is the motion he made:
Then he read the charge. Reference was also made to statements made by the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen, found on page 4826 of Hansard of June 17, 1959. Mr. Meighen said:
On this occasion the proper course undoubtedly has been pursued by the hon. member for West Hastings (Mr. Porter). He has made allegations of conduct against a minister of the Crown, conduct inconsistent with the traditions and honour of parliament, conduct designated as improper in every case where similar questions have arisen in this or in the British house. He has taken the full responsibility, and in a speech temperate in tone and very fair in every respect has laid his charges and made his motion.
The motion is the right motion. The privileges and elections committee historically is the committee which always deals with any contested questions affecting the privileges of parliament. There has never been a case in our history where, a charge being formally laid, the full responsibility being taken and a reference to this committee asked for, such a request or such a resolution has been negatived.
I should like to repeat the phrase "the full responsibility being taken". I think there is only one conclusion that one can draw from that, and that is that if a member makes a charge, he is putting his seat on the line.

He said: Madam Speaker, I am happy to introduce for second reading Bill S-23, the purpose of which is to incorporate the Jules and Paul-Emile Leger Foundation. As Madam Speaker will know, this bill was passed by the Senate on July 9, 1981. It was introduced for first reading in the House by my colleague, the Minister of Communications (Mr. Fox), on July 14.
The bill will create a private corporation, a foundation, to act in the many areas of philanthropy which were dear to the hearts of Jules Leger and which continue to be dear to the heart of Cardinal Paul-Emile Leger. One main object of the foundation is to relieve sickness and hunger and to provide assistance to all in need, including orphans, lepers, the aged, the handicapped and the ill-treated. I must also mention Gabrielle Leger, whose energy and enthusiasm have been an inspiration to this country and who has helped people in Canada and other countries achieve a better quality of life. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of every member of the Progressive Conservative caucus I speak in favour of the speedy passage today of Bill S-23 from the other place, which would incorporate the Jules and Paul-Emile Leger charitable foundation.
Jules and Paul-Emile Leger Foundation
If there are two Canadian brothers who have given more to their faith, to their neighbours on four continents and to the honour of Canada than these two, Mr. Speaker, I do not know their names.
Let me speak first of our former Governor General. The son of a store-keeping family of St. Anicet, Quebec, he studied at le College de Valleyfield, l'Universite de Montreal and at the Sorbonne de Paris. After a period as associate editor of Ottawa's own Le Droit, he joined our Department of External Affairs in 1940 and became an important part of its most golden age during the post-war period. At various times he was first secretary to our high commission in London; adviser to the Canadian delegation to the general assembly of the United Nations; ambassador to Mexico, France, Italy, Belgium and Luxembourg and to the North Atlantic Council; under-Secretary of State for External Affairs; and, later, under-Secretary of State. In 1973, he was appointed to our highest office, that of Governor General.
The real greatness of this right hon. public servant, however, is perhaps better revealed by his conduct after he suffered such a serious stroke in 1974 that his brother, Cardinal Leger, evidently administered the last rites of the church to him. He recovered, but paralysis had struck both his left side and his speech organs. For three years with the daily help of his beloved and charming wife, Gaby, he forced himself to relearn both of our official languages. His courage and will power was sufficient that in time he could again work full days, visit all ten provinces and the Northwest Territories and provide inspiration for each disabled Canadian, whom individually and as a group he always urged never to despair. His expressed thoughts about Canada and the larger issues in life are profound and timely. Let me, Mr. Speaker, give only four examples.

Western civilization:
But times have already changed; we live now in a different age and its contours are not readily apparent. Western civilization, our civilization, is going around in circles and losing its vigour, as a result of a number of contradictions that have paralyzed its energies. Generations are in conflict because there is no recognition of the other's existence; we are insecure in our affluence; there is abject poverty and enormous wealth; conventional morality has lost its hold, and a desire for primeval purity has taken its place; acts of violence are being committed by those who oppose violence; communications technology is using satellites, while large political entities are going towards increasing regionalization.

On culture:
In Canada we have the beginnings of a culture, but it is not a complete culture. It takes centuries to shape a culture, centuries spent together.
On citizenship:
First, I wish to remain a good Canadian. Second, I want to continue to love the province of Quebec from Ottawa. Third, I want to continue to speak French in congenial surroundings. Fourth, I want to receive from you and your colleagues good government. Fifth, I want to pay taxes, moderately.

December 11, 1981
Jules and Paul-Emile Leger Foundation [ Translation]
On the future of Canada, and I quote:
We are now strong enough and sufficiently numerous and sure of ourselves to choose what suits us, to assimilate it and to add our own mark of originality, thus creating a multicultural civilization ...
It was indeed a national tragedy a year ago when the heart attack that struck him down prevented many Canadians from appreciating the many qualities of our twenty-first governor general. We were all profoundly affected by the loss of this great man. Fortunately, Mr. Speaker, His Eminence Cardinal Paul-Emile Leger is still among us, after spending much of his time and energies with the lepers and handicapped children of Africa.
The cardinal was born in the hamlet of St. Anicet now fully 77 years ago. On Christmas day, 1923, after midnight mass, he resolved to become-
[ Translation]
-a Sulpician priest.
[English] *
After that, he said that life was a succession of miracles: first, the Grand Seminary in Montreal and ordination, then four years of seminary teaching in France, and the first opportunity for missionary work in Fukuoka, Japan, in the impossible years from 1933 to 1939. His war years were spent as pastor of the cathedral parish at Valleyfield in Quebec. Thereafter, he was sent to Rome to work closely with His Holiness, Pope Pius XII, in finding food and drugs for the Italian people.
In 1950, at only 46 years of age, he was named Archbishop of Montreal, and only three years later he became the first Montreal ecclesiastic to become a cardinal. Every night at 7 p.m. for the next seventeen years thereafter, he spoke of the faith by radio to the almost two million adherents of his archdiocese. He was a member of the central preparatory commission of the Second Vatican council from 1962 to 1965, and an architect of its important decree on ecumenism. His stature in the church grew so quickly that he was considered to be a future pope. However, in November of 1967 he astonished many people by retiring at 63 years of age to become a simple missionary priest in Africa. He said:
It has become clear to me that the Lord is asking me for deeds as well as words,
[ Translation]
Four years before, he had founded the movement FAME PEREO (I am dying of hunger), with the aim of collecting funds in order to care for some of the four million lepers in Africa. The Cardinal provided financial assistance to eighty-two leper colonies in twenty African countries. Since 1967, he has been working with lepers and the handicapped in his rehabilitation centre for the handicapped in Cameroon.

The following are but three examples of his expressed thoughts. To Canadian youth: "How will your generation change your lives in order to balance out the millions living in our rich centres of prosperity and the 3 billion dying of disease and hunger?"
On his life's work: "I can only provide the reminder that our prime task in life is to help our neighbour. That is all there is to it, yet it says everything".

His faith:
I take what the Lord gives me each day. I do not burden myself with memories* since they often inhibit one's action. My only concern is to practice what the Gospel preaches.

In short, like Mother Theresa of Calcutta, he is a living saint. Let me close, however, with a prophetic remark made by his brother, Jules, in the presence of the Cardinal in his opening address to Sherbrooke University in 1974, literally only hours before his stroke. He said:
A father had two sons. This was our father. To the one, he gave the gift of speech, to the other, that of silence. To each, he gave the reality of God. He assured them that that gift would enable them to make their way in life. The sons went their ways, the one in the service of the church, and the other, of the state.
On this basis, it is with great pleasure that I would call on all hon. members of this House to pass this measure as quickly as we can. Let us do it today.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure, on behalf of the New Democratic Party, to speak in support of this bill. I quite often think that the activities of our lives obscure the reasons we are here. Speaking to this bill gives us an opportunity to reflect on some of the larger perspectives of life. I am reminded of the story of the passerby of a construction site. He asked three men there what they were doing. One said that he was merely a bricklayer and was laying some bricks; another said he was earning $30 an hour; and the third one said that he was building a cathedral. So it is that if we have larger visions of life, we can motivate and inspire other people. This bill reminds me of that type of vision.
One of my favourite questions when talking with people as I travel to my constituency every week on the plane, or even when talking with some of my colleagues, is this: Can you tell me who you are without giving a job description? We find ourselves so immersed in our activities that we fail to take a look at what our lives have done for others. In life, I think we probably fall into two categories. We can either be builders or wreckers. We can build into the lives of others with our words, deeds, actions and ideas, or we can wreck.
The bill we are discussing today honours two builders. It commemorates two Canadian heroes: the former Governor General, Jules Leger, and the cardinal, Paul-Emile Leger. Let us reflect for a moment on these two Canadian builders. First of all, the former Governor General, Jules Leger, was the

from those who are poor. Quite often we are insulated from those who may be suffering because we have not experienced the type of situation they experience.
Last night as I was going outside the House following the vote one of our friends in the House here, a Member of Parliament, was having difficulty collapsing a wheelchair for another one of our colleagues here who has been hurt. I assisted in collapsing this wheelchair because I had done this for more than three years of my life when working with the Society of Crippled Children and Adults. As I was reflecting on that incident when leaving the House I thought this was a very simple task and I was glad that member had that opportunity, it seemed to me for the first time in his life, of collapsing a wheelchair for another person. I said to myself: This type of awareness is something we need because if we are aware of someone who is going through suffering, someone who is very close to us, we become more responsive to those who have needs.
I hope this foundation in the years ahead will make us more aware of those who have needs, be they handicapped or, as the objects of the bill state, those who might be sick, hungry or ill-treated. As I think of the perspective that is offered here 1 have hope for this foundation, and in closing I would just like to share at least one of my hopes.
At lunchtime I was discussing this particular bill with one of my colleagues, the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mrs. Mitchell). We were thinking of some of the implications this bill might have. We thought how nice, how good and how useful it would be if one of the implications of this bill would be to meet some of the needs of our native children. The Legers had a concern for children and for those who are needy. The plight of our native children is a national disgrace. Native children grow up on reserves that lack basic sanitation. They have no amenities. Even in my own constituency, where I have seven Indian reserves, in this year, 1981, they do not have water and sewer in any of their homes. When we think about the overcrowded and inadequate housing they face, the chronic unemployment and education which lacks native cultural content with few native teachers, when we think of the high incidence of health problems, alcoholism and suicide, we realize this is symptomatic of frustration and despair.
I cannot help but reflect, and hope as we support this bill, that there will be things coming from this foundation, which has very broad objectives and deals with very large areas, to benefit these people. I cannot help but think and hope that there will be an opportunity for addressing some of the concerns we have for those who have needs even here in Canada.
We may often ask ourselves why we need another organization. I always think of that little label I often give to people who I think go that extra mile. I call those people gimpers; someone who is prepared to go the extra mile, to do that little bit extra to provide for the needs they see in a given situation. I hope and trust that this foundation, because of the people that it honours and its objectives which have been set forth, will be the gimper that we need to help our society meet some of the needs that exist.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak very briefly on Bill C-60, but before doing so I should like to take one moment to add a personal tribute to Mr. Jules Leger. I had the honour to serve with him in the Department of External Affairs for a number of years and would not want this occasion to pass without my noting his extraordinary achievements and contribution to Canada.
Turning to Bill C-60, to amend the National Energy Board Act, I would like briefly to describe the amendments and indicate the reasons for them.
Two of the amendments are relatively minor. The change to Clause 2 on page 4 of the bill deletes the words "of acquiring lands and" from the subsection which sets out the terms of reference for the National Energy Board in approving the detailed routes of a pipeline. This change has been made in order to make it clear that there is no restriction on a pipeline company to enter into voluntary agreements with land owners between the time that a notice is served on the owner under Section 75 of the act and the time that the detailed route is approved by the board. Since it was never intended that there should be any restriction on such agreements, this change represents an improvement in the drafting.
A change to Clause 5 on page 6 will alter one of the mandatory terms that must be included in a land acquisition agreement or an arbitration award made between a pipeline company and land owner. The indemnification which the company must provide to the land owner from claims by third parties arising from the operation of the pipeline will not be lost if the damage results from an act of momentary carelessness on the part of the land owner. The amendment will provide that the protection can be lost only through some act
December 11, 1981

of gross negligence by the land owner. Evidence before the Senate committee indicated that this wording is now virtually standard in land acquisition agreements made by pipeline companies.
The change to Clause 5 on page 6 should be read together with the two changes to Clause 5 on page 12 of the bill. Together, these amendments will improve the flexibility available to a land owner in selecting lump sum or periodic payments for his or her compensation. As the bill was formerly worded, a land owner would have been forced to make one choice covering all of the compensation he or she would receive regardless of whether some of the types of damage would lend themselves better to the other manner of compensation. Further, the bill originally provided for a review of the amount of periodic payments only to a land owner whose land was being taken and not to neighbouring land owners whose lands were adversely affected. Both types of land owners will now be able to select a lump sum or periodic payments with respect to any part of their compensation and there will be a review of periodic payments in all cases.
During the debate in this House on the second reading of Bill C-60, two questions as to the interpretation of the bill were raised by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Towers). It will be noted that the amendment to Clause 5 of the bill deals with one of those points, namely, the definition of market value contained in the proposed Subsection 75.19(2) of the act. That amendment will make it quite clear that at the time of each five-year review of periodic payments on the acquisition of land, changes in market value that have occurred since the original agreement or since the last review are to be taken into account in setting the new level of compensation.
The second point raised by the hon. member for Red Deer related to the wording of the proposed Subsection 73(1) of the act. This subsection restricts the jurisdiction of an arbitration committee to claims that arise directly out of the construction of a pipeline or the presence of a pipeline on the land. The hon. member questioned whether this subsection was worded too narrowly in that the phrase "operations of the company", which appears in other sections of the act dealing with the terms of reference of an arbitration committee, such as Subsections 75.1(1) and 75.12.(1), does not appear in Subsection 73(1).
There is a reason for this difference. The phrase "operations of the company" is a very broad one. Claims arising out of such operations could include many types that are beyond the ability of an arbitration committee, which is composed of experts in land evaluation, to decide and which can only be tried by the courts. An example of these might be claims arising out of torts such as highway traffic accidents, defamation or claims for breach of contract other than a contract for compensation for damages to land or even for claims arising out of financial or stock market operations of the company.
It is for this reason that the wording of Clause 73(1) confines an arbitration committee to claims that arise in
National Energy Board Act
relation to a particular pipeline, including leakage of the contents of the line, the activities of the company in building and operating the line and any interference with the use of the land caused by the presence of the pipeline. I am confident that no dispute which should properly be decided by the arbitration committee will be excluded from its jurisdiction.
In conclusion, I urge the House to support the amendments made by the Senate, since each is a clear improvement to the bill. We owe it to those who will be affected by pipeline construction that is now in the planning stages to implement these valuable suggestions.

Mr. Speaker, I also wish to speak about the amendments to Bill C-60, and I do so on behalf of the New Democratic Party. I want to express my appreciation to the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell), our energy critic, who has given me this opportunity to speak about these amendments.
I want to reiterate some of the things brought forward by the hon. member for Calgary Centre (Mr. Andre). We dealt with this bill nine months ago, and during those nine months the residents of the Yahk area have experienced disruption. Over the past nine months the people of Yahk have been the actual builders of Bill C-60. The RCMP went out in riot gear to expropriate land. The lands of four residents were expropriated, but during that time the Northern Pipeline Agency mysteriously came in and resolved the situation for those four land owners. The agency made a commitment which satisfied those four residents.
Let me talk about the rest of the community. There was a will to try to co-operate, even though the people saw what was going to happen to them. In October of 1980 the people affected were given small pittances of remuneration. They were promised that if settlements were made in another area, they would be treated equally.
I visited the home of one of these residents the other day. I was accompanied by a representative of the Northern Pipeline Agency and a representative from Foothills Pipe Lines. I asked those two representatives to look out the window and see what that family had to put up with. The pipeline runs within 50 feet of the building. Road access to their home was cut off. From October of 1980 until December 1981 they have suffered the inconvenience of having machinery about. There has been dust and dirt. Their land has been uprooted. In September two inches of top soil were put down and seeds were thrown on to it. The entrance these people had been using to come in and go out had been destroyed to the point where they could not drive on it. I asked those two representatives how they would react if all this happened to their homes and what they would do if they had to leave their cars outside their property and walk through ditches to a home full of dust and dirt. I wonder how they would react if their property were expropriated or their trees were cut down and they were told the value of those trees would be assessed at a later date. These are the kinds of outrageous things that are going on.
Even though these people were allowed to participate in the program, expropriation liens were put on their properties. It has now been agreed that they will be removed.
The pipeline also crossed a creek called Hawkins Creek, a traditional water supply. That has been disrupted, and no one will undertake to help resolve that problem.
There is very little topsoil in the Yahk area, but did Foothills save the topsoil? Did Foothills put it aside, dig gravel and backfill with gravel and then put a little topsoil on top? No, that would be too costly. Foothills dug it up, mixed it up, finished laying the pipe and put all tht material back in, and that was it. Can hon. members imagine what the farmers of that area are thinking? They are told there is no topsoil
available for the 150 foot strip through their properties. If there is no topsoil available to the Northern Pipeline Agency, I suppose it is not available to the farmers either. That topsoil was very valuable to the farmers because of fertilizer build up over the years.
I hope the minister will stand by his word. When we were debating this bill at an earlier stage, he said these people would be properly represented, that the provisions of this bill would be retroactive and that the people would be given the opportunity to come back and discuss their problems. The minister said these people would be reimbursed or their land brought up to proper standards. That is the least the people should expect and I think it is only fair. If there is any fairness for the four families whose properties were expropriated and if the minister takes into account the value of the gravel involved, then surely to goodness the value of the topsoil removed and the lawn damage should also be taken into account since this is a matter of great significance to the people affected.
Those are the kinds of hardships that have been created because of the delay of this bill. The government has a responsibility to those who have had to suffer. I would like a commitment from the government that it will bring in this bill when it is finally adopted by the Senate and instruct these people to come into the area and hold hearings. Hopefully people will be treated in the proper way provided in the bill. A commitment was given that they would have that opportunity and that the rest of Canada would enjoy the provisions of this bill.
The Conservative Party talks about the freedom to own land. I did not see any Conservative member stand up and try and protect the rights of those individuals which are being infringed upon. Where were the Conservatives at that time? Was it because it was the Foothills Pipe Lines that was involved? Could that have been why we did not hear from the Conservative Party in an attempt to protect the rights of these individuals? I certainly congratulate my party, the NDP, for standing up and being counted and saying that there has been a violation.

Mr. Speaker, I will not delay the House very long. The hon. member for Calgary Centre (Mr. Andre) did not take long when he was speaking.
When this pipeline becomes a reality, quite a bit of mileage of it will pass through the constituency of Bow River. There has been considerable concern on the part of many people there and I want to voice one or two of those concerns.
There is one part of this bill that I like very much. If the company does not make a proper award, it goes to arbitration and if the arbitration board rules that it exceeds 85 per cent of the amount offered, all legal fees must be paid by the company. That is proper.
In the Alberta department of highways we worked on the principle that it was a house for a house. When land was disrupted, it had to be left in at least as good a condition as it was found. I have seen rocks, gumbo, black loam, bottles and debris ploughed into the land. There has been no concern for the land owner at all. I hope there will not be a repeat of that type of situation when the pipeline goes through. It is a matter of taking this to the company.
When we had a situation like that, I asked the company man to take a look at it. It was corrected immediately to the satisfaction of the land owner. It is not right when people take advantage of a land owner, thinking that he is only a farmer, that he has no friends and cannot go to court so we will plough our way through, ruin his land and give him the very least possible. I hope that will not be the attitude of those building this pipeline. It is not the attitude of the Alberta government when taking land for highways or other purposes.
One member said that it is a case of stockpiling black dirt. It is an extra expense, but it is an expense charged to that work. It is a bother, a nuisance and a rip-off of black soil, but black soil is a wonderful thing. It is that six inches that feeds the world. We cannot afford to lose that two, three or six inches of black dirt, wherever it happens to be. The Alberta department of highways has an insistent clause: The construction company must stockpile that black dirt. After the work has been done, the soil must be put back.
An experiment was carried out in Alberta. After one year the land did not look that great, but after three years of proper work it was back to the same condition it was before it was disrupted. The crops now grow just as well as previously. We cannot afford the loss of good farmland in this country. There is too little of it now. Farmers should not be expected to bear the brunt of the cost of a large project such as this pipeline. It should be paid for by all the people of this country and the United States, not by just the land owners. When a pipeline is built across a farmer's land, whether it is an acre, quarter section, section or several sections, he should be compensated for the amount of grain he would have grown on that land for many years into the future. That is not asking too much. That is simply being fair to our farmers.
I hope that those who construct the pipeline will be fair to the farmers and not only to those who put up the capital. Farmers are generally reasonable people. I have had some

difficult situations to deal with but never once was I not able to go to the farm, stand on the land affected and make a settlement. No matter how irate the farmer is, he is still reasonable.
All the farmer wants is that the land be put back the way it was before so that he can continue to produce food for the world and support his family. This is a wonderful opportunity for the companies involved to show they have some human interest by ensuring that when they disrupt a farm, they will put the land back in at least as good a condition as it was before they appeared on the scene.

With all due respect to the hon. member, the Chair has to be guided by the procedures of the House.
Clause 2 reads as follows:
In this Act,
"meat" means fresh, chilled and frozen beef and veal;-
That is carefully defined in the clause.
There are two amendments offered in the name of the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Neil). In the opinion of the Chair, they introduce a new definition to Clause 2 which is an amendment of a substantive nature to the interpretation clause.
On this point, Beauchesne's fifth edition, paragraph (10) of Citation 773 states as follows:
A substantive amendment may not be introduced by way of a modification to the interpretation clause of a bill.
For this reason, the opinion of the Chair is that Motion No. 1 is not acceptable.
The principle of the bill, as enunciated in the long title and in the Royal Recommendation concerns meat which is explicitly defined in Clause 2 as "beef and veal".
Motion No. 2 and, for that matter, Motion No. 1 are concerned principally with the insertion of a new element, namely lamb into the bill.
For the benefit of the hon. member, I also refer him to Beauchesne's fifth edition, paragraph (1) of Citation 773. Consequently, because Motion No. 2 extends the purposes of the bill beyond its scope, the Chair must rule it out of order.
