He said: I want to say, Mr. Speaker, that I should make a comment about many things concerning meat production in Canada. I will be as brief as I possibly can. I will probably not cover all aspects of the subject, which many of the members would like me to put on the record today, because of lack of time.
I am sure that all members of the meat industry, as well as Canadian consumers, will be pleased to see this bill finally enacted into law. I am sure the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Neil) would say that if he had included that other group in it, they would also be pleased.
The proposal for a meat import law was widely discussed before the act was drafted. There was a lively debate at second reading and the bill was thoroughly debated in committee. Also in committee, provisions were made for the interested parties to present their views, and many organizations took advantage of that opportunity.
I think 1 can safely say, Mr. Speaker, that this bill represents the best thinking on the subject by all parties concerned. I believe it will help a great deal to assist the beef industry and to provide consumers with the assurance that adequate supplies of red meat will always be available at reasonable prices.
Canada is the only major beef importing country in the world that has not had an ongoing beef import policy. Without such a policy, we were vulnerable to market distortions and international price swings which are beyond our control. The ad hoc import quotas, which we have been applying on a periodic basis, have led to uncertainties, both for our trading partners and for the Canadian beef industry. With this act we now have permanent controls in place.
Canada is both an importer and an exporter of beef. About 90 per cent of imports are from New Zealand and Australia and are primarily for manufacturing or the lower end of the hotel, the restaurant and the institutional trade. The other 10 per cent comes from the United States and is primarily high quality cuts for the deluxe hotel and restaurant trade.
In 1980 Canada imported 115 million pounds of beef and veal and exported 100 million pounds. In terms of export, the United States of America is by far our most important customer, buying nearly 92 million pounds.
Bill C-46 roughly parallels the U.S. Meat Import Law, including the counter-cyclical formula which allows for lower import quotas when domestic production is high, and higher import quotas when Canadian production is low. This will allow Canada to remain an integral part of the North American livestock economy.
I want to comment briefly, Mr. Speaker, on the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Moose Jaw to have lamb included under the provisions of the act. This matter was discussed in committee and the answers were given at that time. Just last month we reached an agreement with New
Meat Import Act
Zealand to suspend all shipments of chilled lamb carcasses for the next 12 months. This should give the Canadian industry time to study the situation, and we always have access to the safeguard provisions of the Export and Import Permits Act which can be used in an ad hoc fashion in the event of any disruptions in the importation of this product that can be disruptive to our domestically-produced products market. We must increase lamb production in Canada. Although the sheep industry in Canada is expanding at a significant rate, Canada still relies on imports for 80 per cent of its lamb consumption. I believe the market for Canadian lamb could be considerably strengthened and expanded through improved marketing mechanisms and market development activity.
I might also add that if we were to try to include lamb in the act now, it would mean working out a formula to guide import levels, and that would further delay the bill.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO REGULATE IMPORTATION OF MEAT
speechtext: It would not delay the bill one bit, and the minister knows it.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO REGULATE IMPORTATION OF MEAT
speechtext:
The hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Neil) did not include in his amendment any criteria for import levels. The proposal of the hon. member would provide for a control to be placed on imports of lamb, but he failed to mention any criteria which could be used to establish import levels. In other words, no formula was proposed to establish import levels because the circumstances and criteria under which lamb imports are to be controlled were not spelled out. The producers and consumers were not given any assurance regarding the predictability of lamb imports. Even New Zealanders cannot promise that under present world market conditions and considering the demand for their product.
In the past, the beef industry has had little opportunity to comment on annual beef import levels before they were put in place. As I said, the industry has been awaiting this legislation for a long time. Under the meat import act there will be an advisory committee that can examine the relevant information and advise the minister before he makes a decision on the import level for the coming year. The advisory committee will consist of representatives of a cross-section of the beef marketing chain, from producer to consumer. I expect that I will be inviting members of the Canadian Cattlemen's Association, the Canadian Association of Consumers and the Canadian Meat Council, among others, to serve on the committee.
This legislation, which clearly spells out the criteria under which beef imports will be controlled, should provide cattle producers with greater confidence. At the same time, consumers will have access to world supplies of beef at times when Canadian supplies are not sufficient to serve the market. Over time, the act will help to stabilize both supplies and prices.
As I said before, the act will not answer all the questions of Canadian beef producers. One of the main concerns in the many letters I have received is that they want control of imports of live cattle coming into our market, which can be very disruptive to the supply position in slaughtering opera-

December 11, 1981
Meat Import Act
tions in Canada. We saw this happen last year. We predict that it will happen again this year. This act does not have anything to do with live cattle. I make that very clear, but I know most hon. members in the House are aware of this. It is one of the most unpredictable problems which they face, especially when imports from another country can take over as much as 18 per cent of the slaughter market in the country. This is not per day, per week or per month; this is for several months in the year. This does not happen in any other country in the world. For example, in the province of Ontario imported live cattle took over 25 per cent of the slaughter market for over four months. One could imagine what would happen in the United States of America, which is where these cattle come from, if someone took over that high a percentage of its market. I am sure it would not be allowed for very long.
Earlier, I talked in the House about one of the American states passing a law which was a non-tariff barrier. This act will be disruptive in the potato market in the country if it is allowed to continue. If we go through the procedure of GATT hearings and appointing an independent court of review, commission of review or whatever, it will take some time to rectify what has been done by the state of Maine. It is controlling the imports into the United States, which is contrary to the international trade agreement. Before we even started to draft this act before us, hon. members and people who appeared before the committee were well aware of the views of some of our trading partners.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO REGULATE IMPORTATION OF MEAT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO REGULATE IMPORTATION OF MEAT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will be very brief in my remarks today in view of Your Honour's ruling. I find it almost incomprehensible that only in the Parliament of Canada is lamb not meat; it is absolutely unbelievable. I listened to the minister's few comments. He said that if we included lamb in the bill, it would require considerable work to draft some of the clauses. He also said that it would cause delays and that there is no formula. The amendment does not require a formula. The amendment which I put forward provided for the very thing which the minister arranged earlier this year when he issued a news release indicating that the agreement between the New Zealand Meat Producers Board and the Canada Sheep Council was a voluntary agreement to restrict and suspend until Easter 1982 the shipment of lamb into the country.
I do not believe that the minister is really interested in the welfare of Canadian farmers. The Canada Sheep Council appeared before the committee. It made representations to him. It told him what was the problem, but he turned a deaf ear. I am absolutely shocked that the minister is not prepared to include lamb and to protect the lamb producers of the country. It is an infant industry. These people are trying to build up a sheep and lamb-raising industry. They have had many problems over the years. They were at their peak in 1940, and by 1978 they were getting well into the business. During the last three years the sheep industry in Canada increased by 30 per cent. Then they ran into difficulties
because New Zealand was importing fresh chilled lamb into Canada at a time when the market was at its peak. It depressed the market, and lamb producers were selling lamb at less than the cost of production. We had an opportunity to help this new industry, but it did not happen.
I will not say anymore, but I suggest that if the industry has difficulties, it is no one's fault but the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) and the government he represents.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO REGULATE IMPORTATION OF MEAT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to make a short intervention on third reading of Bill C-46, but before doing so I want to make a brief comment about the subject of lamb and sheep imports, as well as our Canadian industry. Perhaps it was because there was no meat import bill about 40 years ago that the lamb and sheep industry in Canada has been in continuous trouble. It was a thriving industry prior to the last war. I was surrounded by four large sheep outfits on my cattle ranch, but their downfall began with the lack of good Scots sheep herders who spent their lifetime herding sheep. When it became difficult to attract them from Scotland, the industry began to have problems. Its real problems began soon after the war because of the importation of much cheaper lamb and mutton from Australia and New Zealand. As a result, in Canada we are still consuming less than two pounds per capita of lamb and mutton per year. This amount is almost negligible, Mr. Speaker. If legislation like this had been in place 40 years ago, perhaps we would still have in Canada a major lamb, sheep and wool industry. However, as the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Neil) said, it is coming back.
We in the official opposition fully support Bill C-46, Mr. Speaker, and urge final passage of it this afternoon. My remarks and those of my colleagues will be very brief, I can assure you.
First of all, I should like to make some appropriate background comments. Canada's beef cattle industry has recommended and worked hard for beef, or meat import legislation since 1970. My interest in this subject began two years before I became politically involved in 1972, and I might add that my motivation was partly the need for this kind of legislation in 1970.
In 1970 the Canadian Cattlemen's Association first proposed this type of legislation at a meeting with the then minister of agriculture, the Hon. Bud Olson.
If there was ever any doubt about the need for and the propriety of such legislation, that was entirely removed in 1976 when Canada, and especially our domestic beef-cattle industry, was completely overwhelmed with offshore beef imports from Australia and New Zealand. At that time, those offshore beef imports had unrestricted access to Canadian markets and they were coming in at prices well below those of the same products imported to the United States. It was also a time in our cattle production cycle when we were producing an alltime record amount of domestic beef.

December 11, 1981

The years 1975 and 1976 were truly disastrous for the Canadian cattle industry because of those unrestricted imports coming into our markets on top of our own record high domestic supplies. In many respects, our cattle industry has never fully recovered from that disaster because there is no genuine incentive, to stay in or go back into or start up a beef-cattle operation in Canada. There is no confidence in the political direction of this government in so far as the long-term future of our cattle industry is concerned. It is to be hoped that this new legislation, a first of its kind, will help change that situation.
I would be remiss indeed, if I did not remind the House of the background contribution to this legislation made by this party's beef import consultative committee during the late summer of 1979. I was privileged to be chairman of that committee, and I recall very well the valuable input it received from cattle producers and many related people in the industry.
The legislation before us today contains the essential elements that emerged from that consultative committee over two years ago. Although our standing committee study of the bill was split over the summer recess, it was a good session in committee.
It is appropriate to commend the input to that committee by the Canadian Cattlemen's Association. Their presentation was easily the most in depth and carefully researched to come before it. That is quite understandable, in view of its 11 years of effort and support for this kind of legislation. We should be particularly grateful to the Canadian Cattlemen's Association for the improvements it suggested to the quota formula that is now part of the bill dealing with forward projections of cattle numbers. The association pointed out how difficult that exercise would be, and the bill has been improved.
As I have already indicated, the greatest potential benefit of this legislation will be the restoration of some badly needed confidence in the long-term viability of Canada's beef cattle industry. Furthermore, this new legislation will be visible evidence that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) is sensitive to the situation in the beef-cattle industry and that he does indeed care.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I have a brief comment about the state of our cattle industry as we approach this year end. Our industry is indeed in a nation-wide crisis in all sectors of cattle and beef production. In some respects it is a crisis even more serious than that of the 1930s-and I will quickly expand on that-because there are now many more farmers, especially cattle producers, who are losing their farms and ranches due to forced sales, to bankruptcies and to bank foreclosures. These and other related problems come about as a result of the difficulties experienced with cash flow, or, more properly, lack of cash flow. At least in the 1930s we survived in many cases without any cash flow by simply living off the land.
The cattle industry is presently undergoing a critical examination and evaluation by three different agencies. First of all there were the public hearings held by the Senate's agriculture committee following its working paper on alternatives to marketing and stabilization for our beef industry. That committee
Meat Import Act
concluded its public hearings last Wednesday in Ottawa, and I was privileged to present some of my personal views there.
The second ongoing event is the questionnaire sent out by the Minister of Agriculture over his signature to 140,000 cattle producers, including 53,000 dairy producers.
Third, there is the minister's two-man investigative committee which, I understand, has completed the physical investigation and is now in the process of preparing a report.
The minister has made it very clear to me that he will not make any public statements indicating what the federal government's program might or might not be in relation to the Canadian cattle crisis until after the three exercises are over and the reports are in. That is understandable and it is fair.
I conclude by urging the minister to use the stabilization legislation that has been on the books in amended form since 1975-and he has used it already on several occasions-in order to bring in a national, harmonized stabilization program for the cattle industry that involves the three sectors that should be involved, that is, the federal government, the governments of the cattle provinces and the cattle producers and feeders on a voluntary basis.
I can only suggest that if they are all approached and brought together, there will be an understanding and a will to do something about the situation in which we find ourselves now in spite of the provincial programs that are becoming a little too numerous. In case there is any misunderstanding, such a national stabilization program would in no way involve a marketing board with or without supply management.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO REGULATE IMPORTATION OF MEAT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO REGULATE IMPORTATION OF MEAT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to take a few minutes to comment on third reading of Bill C-46, the meat import legislation. This idea has been around since the early 1970s and a great many organizations have favoured some form of import law for meats. I am afraid that a great many of those organizations will be disappointed with this particular development, but it is better than nothing.
For that reason, we will tend to give it some support, with the reservations that I would like to spend a few minutes outlining. It seems to me that what we are doing with the meat import law is generally recognized by most economists who have been dealing with the issue. In effect, we are dealing with a form of supply management. We are attempting, with an import law, to restrict the amount of meat and, in this case, restrict only beef. In the House of Commons, "meat" means only beef and frozen veal. However, it is a recognition that there is a requirement, on occasion, to interfere with the free market system and with the free exchange of goods. In 1976, when imports almost doubled, this was brought to the attention of even the most rabid free enterpriser. We now have fairly wide-ranging support and a minimal attempt at supply management.

December 11, 1981
Meat Import Act
In pure, theoretical market or economic terms, the countercyclical idea is a strictly philosophical concept which cannot be found in real life. Our beef cycly runs similarly to that of Australia, which runs similarly to that of New Zealand. Any attempt to pretend to implement a counter-cyclical formula will not result in a change in the cycles in those countries. They will not reduce production when our production is at a high point, and they will not produce more beef at times when ours appears to be declining. They will react to the same economic forces on a worldwide basis as those to which we have been reacting, and their overproduction periods will occur at pretty much the same time as our periods of overproduction.
By restricting this meat import bill only to beef and to some classes of veal, the government is telling us in advance what it really thinks of this particular industry. At the beginning of 1981, the government opened the quotas wide open. We had a form of quota which had been in existence for the past decade or so. However, this year, when the cattle cycle was at a point when there probably should have been a quota, the government decided to have no quota at all. As a result, because New Zealand and Australia are at a low point in their production cycles, they did not send us very much meat, but we did receive about one million pounds of European meat into the country. Presumably, these historical imports will become entrenched in practice and will give these countries a foot in the door of our markets, while we find it very difficult to gain entry into their markets.
Meanwhile, back on the farms and ranches of this country, cattle producers are dying a very painful death owing to low prices for beef. This is supposedly the signal to tighten up imports under any counter-cyclical law, but our borders are still wide open. Not only are they wide open, but, as well, during the last round of the GATT negotiations, the New Zealanders were able to gain guaranteed access to this country's markets, which probably overrules the bottom end of the import quota from three to five years out of ten years, depending on whose set of outlook figures one uses. Therefore, the door has been permanently propped open for these imports outside of this law, and the guaranteed minimum access agreements under GATT override this law. Therefore, the law itself will only be in effect from five to seven years out of ten years.
I can say that both parties in opposition did try to improve this bill. We were prepared to support the attempt of the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Neil) to include lamb and mutton in the law. We had also proposed that under the law we should have a board, which would monitor and take responsibility for bringing imports into this country so that producers in Canada would be assured that imports would not be brought in at prices lower than the domestic price. That is not a new concept. The Canadian Dairy Commission does that with butter and cheese. We thought that it would only be fair if Canadian meat producers had the same kind of protection. Unfortunately, the government refused to pick up that option. Under the rules of the House and of the committee, as Your
Honour knows, such substantive amendments were ruled out of order.
We think that, short of a miracle or a concentrated drive on the part of the Government of Canada and the provinces, the meat industry in this country is in for very difficult times at the producer level. We think there is a clear need for a kind of meat marketing policy which will include all of the red meats, poultry and eggs in one commodity board which can make progressive plans which will be of use to all of these sectors in the meat industry, instead of setting up separate agencies on boards so that one is picking at the other's market.
We think that this is the only way to rationalize the meat industry in a manner which will be of use to producers in this country and which will provide consumers with the plentiful supplies of meat and poultry products. We think that this bill goes only a little way toward that objective. We think it is a very small, tiny, baby step toward the kind of meat marketing authority that the producers in this country have been demanding and require. We think its only use is to demonstrate a willingness to consider a feeble attempt at supply management. Because the bill is making that attempt to control supplies of meat which come into the country and therefore control supplies available on the domestic market, we will grant our support to the bill and wish it a speedy passage.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO REGULATE IMPORTATION OF MEAT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is an important bill for the Canadian cattle industry. I am very pleased to have an opportunity this afternoon to say a few words in the final stages of third reading of this bill. It is a great relief to many of us that we in this country will finally be getting a meat import law. We went through the meat definitions earlier, and I will refer to that later if I have the time. However, it is a great relief that we will have this piece of legislation.
We on this side support the bill, but we support it with some reservations. I am glad to see the minister is here this afternoon, and I would like to point out to him why we have some reservations concerning the bill.
The hon. member from the NDP who spoke previously said that it is a feeble attempt at supply management. It is very much of a feeble attempt at supply management for two reasons. The hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Hargrave) who spoke earlier has been involved with this bill for over ten years, which is a testimony to the ability of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) to get minimal things through his cabinet so that we can have some protection for the beef industry in this country.
To paraphrase the minister, he said that Canada is the only major beef importing country which does not have some kind of policy which restricts imports into this country. We all know that, and we have been telling him that in this country for the last ten years. It seems ironic, when we do get a bill which will protect imports in this country, that it will be largely symbolic because of the way we were forced to accept the guaranteed minimum access level to which reference was made earlier this afternoon. The meat import law which is in front of us will not
December 11, 1981

be able to do the kind of job that it could have done had we had better representations on behalf of the Canadian cattle industry at the latest round of the General Agreements on Tariffs and Trade. It seems ironic that at that meeting we were represented by the then Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce who was from western Canada and who was in the cabinet. If anyone should have known what was involved in the guaranteed minimum access which Canada granted to its trading partners in GATT, it should have been that minister. However, what did happen, to quote some figures very briefly, is that as a result of negotiations at GATT, Canada agreed to accept approximately 10 per cent to 15 per cent more beef on a per capita basis than the Americans accepted. What that means is largely that this bill will be ineffective. It will be even worse than that. Had the bill been in operation for the last two years, the beef import law formula would not have come into effect at all. When we have a situation in which the formula does come into effect, it will mean that Canada will again be accepting more beef on a per capita basis than will the Americans. I give notice to the minister that what will happen then is that live cattle will be displaced out of Canada into the United States, causing problems with regard to our trading relations with the Americans. We experienced this in 1976 when they closed the border, not only to beef but to pork as well.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO REGULATE IMPORTATION OF MEAT
speechtext: You should have taken them to GATT.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO REGULATE IMPORTATION OF MEAT
speechtext:
The minister says we should have taken them to GATT. Why didn't he take them to GATT? He is the Minister of Agriculture responsible for the total industry across the country. If he felt strongly enough about it and could convince his cabinet colleagues that this was the proper thing to do to protect the beef industry which he represents from one end of this great country to the other, he should have taken them to GATT. He would have received total support from the agricultural community. It is easy for him to sit in the House now and say that we should have taken them to GATT, implying that he is a good fellow, but why didn't the minister take them to GATT at the time? We would have been very pleased to see that happen, and the minister would have received tremendous support from the agricultural industry. In that regard, I wish he would think of those things at the time they happen and go to bat then for the Canadian beef industry.
Let me refer to a study done by the Senate Standing Committee on Agriculture. The report was released in October 1977. The first time I ever came to Ottawa was to appear before that committee. At that time, some five years ago, it was universally agreed that a beef import law, or a meat import law patterned largely after what the Americans were doing, would have been beneficial to the beef industry. As the minister pointed out in his remarks on this bill earlier on, we know this bill is not going to be a panacea, something which solves all the problems of the industry, but it is one thing that would have helped a tremendous amount had it been in
Meat Import Act
existence five, six or seven years ago. We could have had a meat import law in effect at that time that contained a formula that would have worked without being subject to the guaranteed minimum access levels. These are the kinds of things that are on this minister's head when it comes to making this meat import law as effective as possible for Canadian beef producers.
I cannot emphasize too strongly how badly the industry was served by a previous Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce who was a cattleman from Alberta. If anyone should have known what would have been acceptable, workable and helpful to the Canadian beef industry, which is largely located in his province, it was him, yet he was the minister who was responsible for seeing that we agreed to very damaging guaranteed minimum access levels under the agreement that was signed. That points out how important this present Minister of Agriculture has been in terms of influencing his cabinet colleagues in relation to legislation to protect the Canadian agricultural industry in general and, in this case, specifically the beef industry.
Despite all the reservations we have about this measure in terms of its ability to function and do the job intended, we very much support the bill. We have to give credit to the government for accepting two amendments at committee which I think will make the bill much more workable. The main amendment is an amendment that makes better use of the formula mechanism. It gives it a much more responsive base figure for deriving quotas. That is going to be more beneficial to the industry. We have to give the government credit for accepting that amendment, and I mean that in all sincerity. I think everybody would agree that this is a very good amendment.
The other amendment was a minor one in terms of seeing that the advisory committee is sufficiently staffed in the event that one of the members is unable to attend, for whatever reason. That is a good amendment and I think the minister should be pleased that everybody agreed that it should be at the minister's discretion whom he appoints. In that sense we have confidence in the Minister of Agriculture having the discretionary power to appoint people to serve on that committee if somebody is unable to attend for health reasons, personal family reasons, or for whatever other reason.
Our major criticism in terms of this measure is that we did not have it in 1974, 1975 and 1976, as was pointed out by the hon. member for Medicine Hat. At that time the Canadian industry was literally being clobbered by offshore New Zealand and Australia beef. At that time beef that stood on docks in Australia and New Zealand commanded a different price simply because of different destinations. There was a difference at that time of some 25 cents to 30 cents a pound for imported beef originating from the same source but landing in Montreal and New York. That was simply because Canada was the only major importer of beef around the world that did not have some form of import protection.
The general view of the cattle industry at that time was that we did not favour any kind of restrictions. The quickest way to

December 11, 1981
Meat Import Act
get rid of the surplus is to let the market absorb it at whatever price it can be absorbed at, getting rid of the surplus, getting it out of the way so we can get back into a profitable price situation.
What did happen at that time was that the European Economic Community totally cut off the importation of any beef. There were boats literally in the middle of the ocean, yet the European Economic Community simply would not allow them to unload their cargoes of beef. This small country of Canada, with something like 20 million people and a per capita consumption that is less than that of the United States, was left as the only country in the world of any significance in terms of imported beef without import restrictions of some kind. We had no choice but to ask for import restrictions.
Perhaps the minister will remember an opportunity I had, along with colleagues from Manitoba at the time, of meeting with him in the middle of winter on a very cold February evening in Winnipeg. We tried to impress upon him our need for some kind of protection against the vast amounts of meats coming in from Australia and New Zealand. The minister did not see fit to do anything about this until almost the end of 1976 after we had suffered through two very bad years as far as imports are concerned. At that time he brought in import restrictions under the Export and Import Permits Act, which he could certainly have done a lot sooner.
There are all kinds of empirical and statistical evidence to suggest that because we were importing low quality cow-beef in vast quantities, the finished beef market here in Canada was depressed. What did happen in terms of being contra-cyclical was that more people sold off more cows than they should have when the price was depressed more than it needed to be because we were bringing in extra supplies of beef from offshore. The whole industry suffered more than it would have had we had some protection such as we are providing today. The industry suffered more than was needed and, consequently, has taken longer to get back on its feet.
The industry is caught now, as are most industries, in a terrible situation as far as the total economy is concerned. People are now saying that the cure-all as far as the cattle industry is concerned is a supply management system allowing the government to regulate the supply of beef through quotas. This has all kinds of implications.
It is wishful thinking on the part of the minister if he thinks he can bring in a supply management system for beef which will help in the short run in the next six months, eight months or a year, which I suggest is the period of time when the industry needs help. First of all it will be a massive job to bring in any kind of program that involves supply management and quotas for the beef industry.
Those of us in western Canada where three-quarters of the beef herd is located could make a very good argument that when the industry suffers, those who suffer the most and soonest are the cow-calf operators. The feed lot industry suffers as well. The whole industry is in trouble. However, in
order to stabilize and formulate long-term solutions to the problems in the industry, the situation with the cow-calf operators must be of primary concern.
In addition to the bureaucratic nightmare which could result from a supply management system for beef, the concern of western Canadian producers would be that its borders would be closed to the United States. This would be detrimental to us in western Canada because the United States provides an outlet and safety valve for many of our feeder cattle and cull cows that go south of the border. At the same time we have a situation in which other provinces are providing subsidies to attract the beef industry into their provinces. That is acceptable, but the difficulties presented to us in western Canada as a result of the closing of the American border would be of major significance, and this question needs to be addressed. If the Minister of Agriculture is interested in giving aid to the beef industry in Canada, he should lead the way in trying to establish a uniform stabilization program across the country. It is evident now that virtually every substantial beef producing province is involved in some way in the support of the beef industry. It is very difficult for my province of Manitoba, where there is a relatively small agricultural community and no vast natural resources or a large industrial base, to support a major part of its economy. Alberta is in a very fortunate position, which we all recognize and approve of, but it makes it more difficult for a province like Manitoba to compete because it does not have the resources or the very large industrial bases such as there are in Ontario.
We should be able to receive leadership from the federal government. However, we have not seen any yet. I am sure the Minister of Agriculture will tell us how he approached the provinces in 1977 with a program which he was willing to implement.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
That Bill C-45, an act to amend the Pest Control Products Act be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Agriculture.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I will not have too much time, but I want to make sure that all members of the House are well aware of the very important role that pesticides have played and still play in the development of this country. They are used widely and effectively in the forest industry and the agricultural industry. They have made life easier for the home gardener and have saved millions of dollars in the control of insect pests and the removal of weeds along public highways, railways and energy corridors.
At the same time, I am also sure that all members of the House are well aware of the growing public concern that chemical pesticides be used properly and be subject to adequate controls.
It has always been the intent of this government, Mr. Speaker, to ensure that the public is fully protected, and for that reason, the Pest Control Products Act was passed to provide my department with the authority to regulate all pesticide products used in Canada.
The amendments now before the House in Bill C-45 represent a reinforcement of those powers in respect of jurisdiction over other government agencies. The amendments are regarded by all those concerned as necessary to clearly define appropriate powers of the federal government over all pesticide matters in Canada.
Let me say that, for many years, my department and, indeed, provincial government agencies have operated under the broad legislative umbrella of the Pest Control Products Act. All people involved in using pesticide products in Canada have followed the act.
But it has been determined by the courts that, in fact, because of the terms and conditions of the act, there were areas of government that were not specifically tied to the Pest Control Products Act. In other words, they were not obliged to operate within its regulations.
Officials of my department have fully discussed the matter with provincial officials and those of other government agencies, and there is complete agreement that the Pest Control Products Act should apply to all those using pesticide products in Canada.
As a result, the amendments are before the House. In essence, they provide a legal basis for jurisdiction that had, until now, been assumed and accepted.

I would also like to draw hon. member's attention to the continuing efforts of researchers in my department to find alternatives to chemicals in the control of pests. They are having remarkable success, both in the discovery of biological controls and in breeding plants that are free of disease and pest resistant.
We will probably never see the day when chemical pesticides will not be necessary, but by using them judiciously as part of an integrated pest management program, the volume of chemicals can be substantially reduced and effective control of pests maintained.

subsubtopic: NARCOTICS CANNABIS OFFENCES
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should reconsider its plan announced in the Speech from the Throne to move cannabis offences to the Food and Drugs Act and to remove the possibility of imprisonment for simple possession and should consider the advisability of leaving cannabis offences as they are in the Criminal Code.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I submitted this motion to the House because, as a concerned Canadian and a father of three teenagers, I was extremely distressed when the government proposed to move marijuana related offences from the Narcotic Control Act to the Food and Drugs Act. Such a move would remove the possibility of imprisonment for simple possession, and the act of possessing marijuana would be changed from a crime to a simple misdemeanour. While the act of smoking marijuana would not be entirely legalized, most people would interpret that to be the case. That is a concern of mine, and there would be grave consequences.
Because of my long involvement with young people and my deep and abiding concern for their wellbeing, I feel very strongly about any move toward leniency in the law where marijuana and other such drugs are concerned. There is a developing trend of evidence pointing to the harmful effects of marijuana. Unfortunately, many-and I could go as far as to say most-people are not aware of this new evidence. How many hon. members are aware of the current medical opinion on marijuana? I venture to say there are only a few. The general public and many parliamentarians have been isolated from these developments. Back in 1972 the LeDain commission of inquiry into the non-medical use of drugs concluded:
The short-term physical effects of cannabis are relatively insignificant on normal persons, and there is as yet no evidence of serious long-term physical effects from use at current levels of consumption in North America.
That was back in 1972. It is indeed unfortunate that many hon. members still refer to the LeDain report as conclusive evidence of the harmlessness of marijuana. Much of what was said in the sixties and early seventies about the harmlessness of marijuana is obsolete and proved untrue. Over the past nine years medical opinion that marijuana "is a harmless substance" or "may be harmfull" has been increasingly altered in favour of the opinion that "marijuana is harmfull". There have been significant changes in the position of the scientific community. Many prominent authorities on the subject who in the sixties and early seventies deemed marijuana harmless are now admitting how wrong they were. I quote Dr. Powelson, who said in 1967:
Marijuana is harmless. There is no evidence that it does anything except make people feel good. It has never made anyone into a criminal or a narcotics addict. It should be legalized.
That was back in 1967. In 1974 Dr. Powelson admitted:
Within five years I knew I was totally wrong ... Medical research groups, after a generation of neglect, began to attribute long-range ill effects to the use of pot. As a result of these findings and my own, I now believe that marijuana is the most dangerous drug we have to contend with today.
This change of opinion throughout the scientific community came about because it has taken time for scientists to complete studies and draw conclusions on the effects of marijuana. It is important to keep in mind, and most pharmacologists agree, that a drug must be presumed harmful until proved otherwise.
I would like to inform the House of what doctors and scientists are telling us today about the damaging effects of marijuana. Cannabis is not a simple drug. The marijuana plant contains many drugs, some of which affect the mind, others which affect the body. THC is the principal psychoactive factor in cannabis responsible for intoxication, although there are at least fifty identifiable, chemically active substances present. As THC and other cannabinoid substances are highly soluble in fat, they tend to accumulate in the brain and gonads and other fatty tissues, and can be expected to persist in the body for a considerable period of time and to accumulate with repeated exposure. THC is removed slowly from the body, and many months are required to recover from its effects. The marijuana user is under the influence of the drug even between highs.
Scientists confirm that cannabis has a number of short-term effects on the brain. There is also significant evidence that continuation over a period of time can produce organic damage to the tissues of the brain, possibly of a permanent nature. Cannabis preparations get in and directly affect brain functions and produce distinctive and irreversible changes. In studies done in England it was found that chronic marijuana smokers aged 18 to 26 had suffered as much brain atrophy as normally encountered in very elderly people. Severe personality changes, memory loss of recent events, hallucinations, and other mental effects were displayed. It was concluded that "regular use of cannabis produces cerebral atrophy in young
December 11, 1981

adults." Anything that adversely affects the brain should not be taken lightly.
Recent findings demonstrate that cannabis inhalation has severely damaging effects on human lung tissue. Chronic cannabis smoking can produce a variety of respiratory difficulties in a year or less, as opposed to ten or twenty years of cigarette smoking. Cannabis smoke is far more damaging to lung tissue than tobacco smoke and renders the lungs more susceptible to infection. Cellular changes in the lung tissue caused by marijuana smoking have been described as "precancerous", indicating that long-term inhalation of marijuana smoke may either directly evoke lung cancer or may at least contribute to the development of lung cancer. Dr. Carol Smith of the Uniform Services University of the Health Services Studies has recently released startling evidence which indicates that chronic use of marijuana may cause disruption of the female menstrual cycle to the point of causing infertility. This is the result of THC interfering with the production of essential hormones.
Other studies by Dr. Ethel Sassenrath of the University of California indicate that the marijuana by-product THC in the bodies of pregnant women is the cause of a much higher incidence of stillbirths and spontaneous abortions. Other recent studies have clearly established that male fertility is also upset by the use of the drug. Users often experience a higher than normal incidence of abnormal sperm, which often is accompanied by reduction in sperm produced. This greatly increased the chance of being temporarily sterile.
The brain, reproductive process and the lungs are not the only body organs and functions that marijuana affects. Medical evidence points to damage to the entire cellular process, chromosome and genetic damage and mutation and suppression of the immune system owing to the use of cannabis. It has also been firmly established that tolerance to cannabis develops, providing a psychological basis for the necessity of the heavy chronic smoker to increase dosage, or to use more potent psychoactive drugs. While marijuana is not physically addictive, there develops a more subtle but no less real psychological dependence that is a formidable obstacle to discontinuance of its use.
So although we may believe that occasional smoking of marijuana is harmless in that we will not become addicted, it is very important to remember that cannabis is a habit-forming substance capable of producing dependence of a pyschological nature.
One person who knows better than any of us the effects of marijuana is Dr. Ingrid L. Lantner of the Erinside Clinic in Willoughby, Ohio. She recently wrote that, in her observation as someone who regularly treats users:
Marijuana is one of the most deteriorating drugs that youth and society has been exposed to!
She explains that few of us or the users recognize the long range consequences. Individuals with symptoms such as fatigue, lack of motivation, depression, paranoia, changed
Narcotics
sexual attitudes and forgetfulness do not realize the cause until after they are totally marijuana-free and have regained their original functions. It is becoming clear that easy accessibility of marijuana is rapidly increasing the number of individuals who have difficulty in leading meaningful, happy and healthy lives. Dr. Lantner concludes:
If we do not do everything possible to prevent its acceptance as a recreational drug, we should stop worrying about the health of our nations in general. Legalization of marijuana will certainly create the impression that this drug is not bad.
I am sure that many hon. members have seen for themselves those who have been smoking up and noted the mindless stupor in which those under the influence seem to exist. Studies have shown that those who smoke marijuana reflect an amotivational syndrome, a massive, chronic passivity, and experience symptoms such as mental confusion, inability to concentrate, diminished attention span, loss of will power, difficulties with concept formation and recent memory, serious loss of motivation, paranoid suspiciouness of others, especially young people of their parents, regression to a more infantile state, distortion of perception and reality, a tendency toward magical thinking, emotional disorders, and I could go on and on. It is quite a list. Is this what we want for our children? I certainly hope not.
As marijuana becomes more common in our society, so does driving under its influence. Millions of people in North America use it and drive every day. Although the scientific community does not know exactly how or to what extent marijuana affects one's driving ability, there is proof that it is dangerous to operate a vehicle while under the influence of marijuana. A Massachusetts study found that 16 per cent of drivers responsible for fatal accidents were stoned on marijuana at the time of the accident. Our unavoidable conclusion must be that doping and driving do not mix.
There is ample evidence that Canadian youth as a collective group are facing unparalleled challenges in the coming decades. We know that any organism is more susceptible to harm when it is growing, and yet efforts to reduce cannabis use by adolescents are minimal and inadequate. Do we want to add to the confusion faced by Canada's young people by changing a law and in the eyes of the young people condoning drug use?
By relaxation of the law, the government is giving the impression that it no longer considers the issue as serious. The interpretation of this by the youth is that marijuana is okay. While the act of smoking marijuana would not be entirely legalized, the vast majority of people would interpret it to be. That is what the problem is. It is a great risk.
If the present trends continue, if adolescent marijuana use increases at its present rate, our society is on its way to acquiring an unmanageable number of emotionally and intellectually handicapped individuals. Regular and daily use of marijuana is not uncommon among the young people of this country. Surveys of high school students have shown rises in direct cannabis experience to the point where by 1979, nearly half the graduates had tried the drug.
14000

A 1978 study by the British Columbia Alcohol and Drug Commission indicated that 47 per cent of 28,000 high school students in Vancouver have used cannabis. Nearly 21 per cent of the students tested indicated cannabis use at least seven or more times in the preceding six months. In Toronto, the most recent survey of the Ontario Addiction Research Foundation found that marijuana had edged out tobacco as the second most popular drug among senior male high school students.
Another 1978 Ontario survey showed that 41 per cent of men between 18 and 20 had smoked marijuana in the previous 12 months. Not a pretty picture, is it? The experience of our American neighbours indicates decriminalization will greatly increase those numbers. There is ample evidence that wherever marijuana has been decriminalized, use and abuse as well as trafficking have drastically increased. Teenage use of marijuana has risen in both Canada and the United States since 1970, but the growth has been higher in those states which have decriminalized marijuana.
In Oregon, the first American state to decriminalize marijuana, a study revealed an increase of 35 per cent in the use in the 18 to 29-year age group from 1974 to 1976. An Oregon police chief suggested why this should not be surprising, in these words:
Adoption of liberalized marijuana laws provides a societal imprimatur that removes the onus from the user and signifies societal acceptance of the practice.
Decriminalization in the state of Maine has demonstrated the dangers of creating the impression among users and potential users that the drug is harmless. The chairman of the Chiefs of Police Association in that state reported in his own community there was a 40 per cent increase in the number of seizures following decriminalization. Alaska and California also report sharp increases in use and trafficking following changes in the law. Is this what we want for our country? This prospect of increased cannabis use must force us also to face up to evidence that heavy users are likely to go on to the use of even more dangerous drugs. Mr. William Pollin of the National Institute on Drug Abuse through studies has concluded that:
-a significant causal relationship exists between the use of marijuana and the use of other drugs.
He found a staggering 73 per cent of heavy users went on to use harder drugs. He also found that people who use marijuana had a thousand times greater chance of going on to heavier drugs than people who did not smoke marijuana.
A front page article in last Wednesday's Globe and Mail revealed that the use of LSD among Ontario high school students rose 67 per in the last four years. In light of Mr. Pollin's conclusions, this House must recognize that the outbreak of this mind-bending drug is largely the result of the casual acceptance and use of marijuana by our youth. Without a doubt, decriminalization will not just lead to higher marijuana acceptance but will unleash a drug abuse problem more severe than we have ever known.
One argument for decriminalization is that people should not be given a criminal record for simple possession. However, to decriminalize marijuana in order to solve this problem would be a drastic overreaction. Decriminalization is not
necessary. Under the Criminal Law Amendment Act of July 15, 1972, it is possible for judges, instead of convicting an accused person, to direct that he or she be discharged absolutely or placed under conditions of probation.
An individual receiving this kind of discharge is not considered to have been convicted of a criminal offence. As well, under the Criminal Records Act anyone convicted of offences concerning cannabis is already eligible for pardon after appropriate periods of good behaviour.
The existence of this legislation allows a judge to use his discretion with a first-time offender. Unfortunately, it is not being consistently applied across the country. In my home province of P.E.I., a first-time offender has a 74 per cent chance of receiving a pardon, while the same offender in Alberta has only a 2.5 per chance of being excused.
Judges who refuse to grant the pardon usually cite the current medical and psychological evidence which I have presented as the reason why they feel bound to impress on young offenders the seriousness of their offence.
The Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) has expressed concern that new legislation is needed in part to act as a guideline for judges and to relieve the heavy burden on the courts which marijuana prosecutions impose. I agree with both of these goals but I must impress upon the House that decriminalization is far too high a price for our young people to pay. The Prince Edward Island Citizens' Council on Drug abuse has made an excellent proposal which will solve these problems and in effect decrease the use of marijuana. This alternative to decriminalization will not saddle the naive user with a record, but it will greatly decrease the number of court appearances, without removing legal sanctions against marijuana use. The change will involve an amendment to the Narcotic Control Act which will give those charged for the first time with possession the option of pleading guilty without going to court. They will, in return receive a full pardon, after completing an in-depth educational program dealing with the medical and psychological effects of marijuana use.
I recognize that not all users will respond to this program. Those charged a second time clearly have developed a habit that is already inflicting its damage. The judges must have the continued authority to use the full measures of the present law to impress on the offender the seriousness of the offence.
I believe so strongly in this proposal that I will soon be presenting it in the form of a private member's bill. It will reflect my belief that the majority of our young people are smart enough, when given the facts, to recognize the dangers of marijuana. But first, the government must acknowledge the dangers and then, respond to it in a reasonable manner. Decriminalization is not a responsible act; it will only shift the responsibility for marijuana misuse off to the pushers and the drug dealers.
I believe that reform of marijuana's legal status at this time will prove detrimental to the youth and society of this country, Mr. Speaker and hon. members. Extreme caution should be

taken when contemplating legislative changes which could have far-reaching effects on our society in general and on our youth in particular. We must educate ourselves and our youth to recognize the hazards involved in cannabis use. This should be the priority, and not the moving of cannabis offences from the Narcotic Control Act to the Food and Drugs Act.

speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker and I thank hon. members. I appreciate the extra time that I have been given. I have been working on this for one year and I am finally having my day in the House.
Before Parliament proceeds to pass a bill decriminalizing the possession of marijuana, let us at least understand and discuss the issues. Let us ask ourselves if we have enough facts to justify such a far-reaching move at this time. Let us understand all the issues before the decriminalization of marijuana gets carved in tablets of stone. If the present trend to drug abuse continues, we will soon acquire, as I mentioned earlier, an unmanageable number of emotionally, intellectually and socially handicapped young people who are unable to function effectively, if at all, in an increasingly complex and demanding world.
I should like to quote Doctor George K. Russell. It was from his excellent book entitled "Marijuana Today" that I have gleaned much of the evidence that I have presented to the House today. I do hope it will give hon. members on all sides of the House food for thought in the consideration of this motion. Doctor Russell writes:
Can the use of marijuana, in any amount, ever be reconciled with the clarity of thought, the personal integrity, and the strength of will, that an individual must have, who would play an active role in helping humanity find the way out of its presently severe and ever-worsening difficulties?
I will conclude my remarks, Mr. Speaker, by saying that, considering the growing volumes of evidence that we have which tells us that marijuana is a harmful drug, if the government is considering decriminalization and it continues to push ahead with its intent to decriminalize, then I say it is wrong. If it were to do any good, Mr. Speaker, I would get down on both my knees in the House and beg and plead with the members opposite to reconsider.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to reply on behalf of the NDP to this motion today. I note that we have been debating agriculture for part of the afternoon. I suppose it is proper that we move from soil to grass. As a matter of fact, hemp-and the Chair will pardon me for that-was part of the agricultural sector of this country for many years before Canada became an industrialized country, for the making of ropes and so on. As a matter of fact, it is true that the government subsidized it for many years. No doubt in this very House of Commons at some point in history
Narcotics
they debated subsidization of hemp, much as we did subsidization of meat and lamb this afternoon. No doubt this country is capable of growing a lot of hemp and a lot of marijuana, if it so wanted. I suppose the question is, what do we want to do about this?
I agree with the hon. member for Malpeque (Mr. Gass) that it is a very important issue. I listened very closely to what the hon. member had to say. He spent quite some time on his speech. I was very interested in what the hon. member had to say. However, in noting that he dealt with the medical evidence and the evidence that he cited, I might tell the hon. member that I was a member of the alcohol and drug commission of the Province of British Columbia for a short period, and I also practised criminal law in the courts of British Columbia for about ten years and dealt with a number of cases of drugs of all sorts. The evidence he cited really deals with the crime of chronic use. I agree with the hon. member that chronic use of almost anything would bring one to a mindless stupor. When the member talked about mindless stupors, diminishing values, suspicion of others and emotional disorders, I thought he was talking about question period in the House of Commons. The hon. member is right in a sense that any chronic abuse obviously creates problems. It is the same for alcohol and tobacco. One can see that around us. One does not need to be a scientist to report that.
As a matter of fact, the problem that we have is that the medical evidence on marijuana is only suggestive and not conclusive. I think it stops far short of proving that heavy, regular use of marijuana may produce lung or heart disease, slow down or halt one's sex life, cause long lasting disturbances of behaviour and brain function, or lower one's resistance to infection.
An authoritative statement from the Addiction Research Foundation points out:
"what is not yet known is the frequency with which these health problems occur among cannabis users, the degree of use needed to produce them, and the percentage of users at risk ... it is probable that any specific health problem due to cannabis will have a low incidence ...
A Gallup poll indicated that about 15 per cent of the Canadian population that is between 2.5 and 2.7 million people, have tried marijuana, and that among younger people between the ages of 18 to 24 the figure is over 25 per cent. Not being a scientist but based on common sense, that would indicate to me that if that many people had used marijuana for a period of time, we would in fact have a lot greater incidence of disease and ill-health than we have, if it caused all the things that the hon. member said it caused. It indicates to me that chronic users may have problems, but occasional users may not have those medical problems.
The hon. member spoke about young people. The problem we have with young people is that they believe what I have just said a minute ago. They think we are trying to scare them. They do not think we are being straightforward with them. I do not think we are either.
I agree with the hon. member that we must find ways to have better drug education programs and alcohol education

programs-that is the biggest drug abuse; but we should also have some way of dealing with our law in a just manner. It has been eight long years in the making, but it appears that the federal government is about to change the present law. This fulfils the promise of 1972, although I am not sure. I looked through some clippings and I noticed some of the headlines were "Ottawa to Ease Marijuana Law within Weeks", in quoting the Minister of Justice (Mr. Chretien) on June 12, 1980. speechtext:
I should like to deal with some of the arguments of the hon. member which are pertinent to the debate. We must ask ourselves whether the state should enforce standards of public taste and common morality. I think that is the first question. It is a difficult one, but I think we decided it in 1968 when the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), the then minister of justice, brought in amendments to the Criminal Code. He talked about the state not having a place in the bedrooms of the nation and so on. It is a debate among criminal lawyers and criminologists. It is Professor Hart on the one side saying that the state has no business; it is to force legality, not morality. It is Sir Patrick Devlin on the other side saying that the state must force morality in order to enforce legality. My view of what has happened in the law in the last 20 years is that the state's business is not to enforce private morality. For example, alcohol is bad but we do not prohibit alcohol; tobacco smoke is bad but we do not prohibit someone from smoking tobacco. Perhaps we do in certain places, but generally we leave it up to a personal choice. Perhaps this is where we should go on the marijuana aspect, providing that it is not hurting other people and that people are not making black market money on it, which, of course, means traffickers.
The second question which we must ask ourselves is whether the classification of cannabis in the Narcotic Control Act is justified. Critics argue that this classification is too strict because cannabis is put in the same legal regime as heroin, cocaine, opium and morphine and it does not have the same properties and same addictive capacities as those drugs. The penalties under the present act are considered too high. For example, seven years' imprisonment maximum for possession, seven years minimum for importing and trafficking, and no discharge or summary conviction for trafficking offences.
Cannabis was added to the Opium and Narcotic Drug Act in 1923, not because of any knowledge of the extent of its use or scientific evidence of harm, but probably on the basis of a book entitled, "The Black Candle" written by a juvenile court judge which included many sensational and irresponsible statements. I appreciate the fact that the hon. member for Malpeque tried to marshal his evidence today with no irresponsible statements, but this has been done too much in the past. There may be arguments that cannabis should not be put in the Narcotic Control Act.
The next question is: How effective is the law right now? We are told that there have been a number of convictions and that they are rising. In 1976, there were 34,000 convictions for simple possession; in 1977, there were approximately 33,000 convictions; in 1978, there were 27,000; in 1979, 27,000. I do not have the figures for 1980, but I suspect they will be substantial. All convictions are registered in criminal records. It is said that there are some 300,000 Canadians who now have criminal records for no other offence than simple possession. One with a drug conviction for possession of even a small amount of marijuana cannot cross the American border. Certainly it has some effect upon these people. In the last year which I cited, 16,970 of those persons convicted were fined; 8,076 were given conditional or absolute discharges; 1,130 were sent to jail, of whom 1,095 were sentenced to less than six months and the remaining convictions resulted in probationary or suspended sentences.
When I was a lawyer in Vancouver I can remember appearing before a judge about five years ago in provincial court. My client had been charged with simple possession. I had been around the courts, I knew the courts. I knew something was wrong; I was about to plead my client guilty, but I let a less experienced lawyer go ahead of me. He pleaded his client guilty. Sure enough, something was bothering the magistrate that day and he gave a 17-year-old young man who had never been in court before, seven days in jail, because he was going to stamp out marijuana. I have heard courts indicate this. For example, I heard the British Columbia Court of Appeal indicate that it would stamp out marijuana in a case which I took before the court. The fact is that they have not stamped it out.
I tend to favour what the hon. member for Malpeque said that there should be more emphasis on educational programs. How effective is the law? The answer to the question is, not very effective. Not only that, it is a discriminatory law.
Tonight there will be parties in Ottawa, Toronto, Montreal, Vancouver and in other big cities. There will be alcohol and

there will be marijuana smoked at those parties. If those people are good citizens in the middle-class and in the upper middle-class, the police will not come to their doors. It will be tolerated by their friends in high places in all walks of life. But who will be arrested tonight? It will be the youth with marijuana in his car. It will be younger people, people who are less able to be protected. It is hypocritical; let us face it, it is a hypocritical law. It comes down hard on a certain segment of our population, but if it came down hard on older or middle-aged people, we would change it pretty quickly. The youth know that the law is harsher on them, they know that they are being discriminated against generally as a group.
The next question is whether cannabis damages health. I personally think drugs damage health, as do alcohol and cigarettes, but the evidence shows that it must be dealt with in chronic proportions. What is the extent of the use of drugs now? I think it is fairly widespread. I cited the Gallup poll earlier. It actually indicated that 46.2 per cent of people between the ages of 18 and 29 have used marijuana. This is a sizeable proportion of our population. By all rights, if we do not change the law and it is illegal, we should seek them out, prosecute them, put them on probation, fine them or put them in jail. This does not make much sense. It seems to me that we are back to the old arguments with respect to alcohol and prohibition.
The final question which should be raised is whether decriminalization will lead to increased use of drugs. It is an important question. It seems to me that the evidence is that the number of cannabis users who progress to harder drugs is only a small proportion of the total number of cannabis users. Moreover, the prohibition against cannabis encourages the progression factor because it requires people to contact traffickers who deal in a variety of drugs. I have defended probably 400 to 500 cases of possession of marijuana. I used to know what happened to some of my clients in later years; I would follow them up. They never progressed to harder drugs. I knew many heroin addicts with whom I dealt. I have talked to them; they came into heroin for various reasons.
In conclusion I want to say that I agree with the hon. member for Malpeque that young people are not stupid. They understand. They know what is going on. They have friends who smoke marijuana and they have friends who abuse marijuana. I agree that when there is abuse at school or at work, disciplinary action must be taken, but I question the effectiveness of the present laws regarding marijuana. It is perhaps a fact that the bad effects of the drug outweigh the good, and the hon. member for Malpeque suggested a number of ways by which we might reduce the problem of drug use.
I think it is plain that minor violations of the law relating to cannabis should no longer carry a criminal stigma or the onerous penalties that currently apply. Nothing less than the minimum concessions proposed by the government should be considered-that is if they are not just idle election promises made to appeal to a certain section of the population, while the
Narcotics
government at the same time refuses to deal with the other section of the population that does not like them. If the proposals for these concessions reach this House, I think they should be welcomed, they should be supported and they should be swiftly passed into law.
Make no mistake; this would not make the use of marijuana respectable. As I understand it, it would only deal with a small amount of marijuana and would eliminate criminal records. That seems to me to make sense.
I smiled when the hon. member for Malpeque quoted some authorities on drug abuse among young people. I began a paper I once wrote on international narcotics control with a quote from an official who said, "The trouble today is that young people abuse drugs; they do not respect their elders and they are not the way they used to be." Mr. Speaker, that was said in 1969, so things have not changed much-the older generation still thinks that the younger generation is irresponsible and that it abuses its health and so on.
I think we have to try to approach the question of marijuana rationally, Mr. Speaker, but we have to approach it. We should welcome a bill that would take at least the minimal step of decriminalizing the possession of small amounts of marijuana. To do less would be hypocritical, and I think our young people know that. We should then say to our young people that abuse of the body, of the self or of the mind is wrong, and we should show them that it is wrong. It seems to me that if we did this, we would have more credibility in their eyes.
My predecessor in Vancouver-Kingsway once made a speech about marijuana which was circulated. It was to the effect that marijuana was the devil's drug, and so on. I watched the reaction of the young people closely. They laughed at it, Mr. Speaker. I do not want them to laugh at the suggestion of the hon. member for Malpeque, and in fact I do not think they will because he put his positions forward very solidly-although I disagree with some of them. I think we both seek the same end, that is, that our young people be healthy individuals who can make a good contribution to society. Still, there are some healthy individuals who are good contributors to our society who have also used marijuana. It does not seem to have affected them particularly, and the young people know that. I think we must make a big effort to establish some educational programs in this regard.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, we must decide what we consider to be the morality of the nation from the particular laws of the nation. I think we have already taken that decision and if we have, we should not have any problem in dealing logically with the government's long awaited reform of the laws that relate to cannabis in this country.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sorry that the hon. member for Malpeque (Mr. Gass) is not in the House as I should like to commend him on the research he has done into the topic now before the House. I agree with many of the things he said. What is perhaps the other extreme

December 11, 1981
Narcotics
was evident in some of the remarks of the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell) who seemed to lean too far the other way. Perhaps that is typical of members on that side of the House.
As the father of four children, three of whom are now beyond their teen years, I have been very concerned about this subject. As head of the family, I have wondered what I would do if one of my children became involved with drugs. I was always proud of my children's scholastic standing, and of their abilty to participate in team sports. When they were at the age where they could become involved in active sports programs, we left the decision up to them. When they decided to participate, we accompanied them to the games so that in fact they were not participating as individuals but the whole family was participating. Sometimes it meant that we had to quit work in the middle of the afternoon in order to go with them, but we did this to show that we were interested in the development of their skills and physical co-ordination. That gave them the encouragement that is so important to any young person involved in sports, whether it be minor baseball or minor hockey.
Over a period of years it was very interesting to notice how they developed even when they were playing atom hockey in the International Silver Stick competition. A group of small town kids won the North American championship two years in a row. This was not only due to their dedication but to that of their parents and the all-round extra effort and team work involved. These kids were not selected from a group of hockey teams to make up a star team. They belonged to a team that played together and developed the co-ordination and team spirit that enabled them to achieve that level. Whether it was in the softball season or the fastball season when they went on to the Ontario playdowns and championships, that keenness of mind and keenness of reflex that is so important to any championship team was always present.
As these children got older, every once in a while I would notice that one was dropping back, not performing as he should. Pretty soon it would be heard that he was doing something that he should not be doing and the standard of excellence was not maintained at the level of the other children who were not experimenting.
I also witnessed the development of these students in schools over many years. In some cases they could not cope and decided to drop out even though they had been top students in the final years of their elementary school and their families had been proud of the way they excelled in their studies as well as in their athletic accomplisments.
It was a terrible schock to me when, in early 1980, I was invited to an elementary school meeting in my constituency which was called by the parents because it was discovered that quite a number of students in grades six and seven were users of the drug cannabis and that someone was pushing that drug at that level. It was a shocking experience to see what had
happened there and how it had wrecked the lives of these young people.
It may be argued by those same young people that alcohol has its ill effects too. However, we must remember that when alcohol is consumed, it is excreted from the body within a matter of hours, whereas cannabis is retained within the system in the fatty tissues of the body. Its effects may turn up several days later in various symptoms usually associated with the judgment and functioning of the mind. I believe that if we looked for examples and statistics, some of which I have heard from those in the medical profession concerning the number of highway traffic accidents which are not related to alcohol but which are related to the use of cannabis or the accumulation of the residue of cannabis in the fatty tissues of the body, we would find them rather shocking.
Certainly, I am not one who believes that this drug should be allowed or made available to young people of our community or to the upper or middle-class, as mentioned by the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway. I normally go home to my family every weekend. I do not get to attend these parties in the capital of Canada on a Friday night.
