I have to go back to my constituents to keep in touch so that I know what is happening in the outside world. However, it would be interesting to know how many convictions there would have been made under the highway traffic act if it could be implicitly proven that many of these accidents were caused by the use of this drug. Even if used several days before, the accumulation of this drug in the body could impair the judgment of a person behind the wheel of an automobile. Certainly, we must admit that although alcohol does not stay in the body for the same extended period of time as the residue of cannabis, alcohol has ill effects if used to excess and can perhaps become just as habit forming. However, I believe that now is not the time to be looking for trends which may open up the accessibility to this drug.
I am somewhat sorry that the hon. member for Malpeque moved his motion in the manner in which he did. I would rather that it had been made very distinctly clear that it should be left under the Narcotics Control Act and, in so doing, ease the level of penalty for a first offence. However, from that time on, it should be made known that if a person is convicted a second time, he can no longer have that criminal record erased, and he cannot go on in society with the profession of his choice. I do not like to think that this might happen to a promising young accountant who must be bonded and cannot have a criminal record. Too many have made a mistake once and have been caught in a situation where they have had to carry criminal records for the rest of their lives. However, they should be given a second chance and some leniency.
It has been nearly ten years since the report of the LeDain Commission. Since that time, we have made tremendous advances as far as plant life is concerned. The yields of wheat have dramatically increased. The yields of other plants such as grains, corn or beans have dramatically increased. In some
December 11, 1981

cases, the protein levels have increased. However, in the same time period, the potency of this drug has also increased by as much as tenfold over what it was at the time of the LeDain Commission report. Therefore, we cannot just go ahead in a hodgepodge situation without some in-depth study. I suspect it is likely that members of the medical profession who belong to this chamber here, one of whom is sitting across the way from me today, will concur with me when I point out that the effects today are far different from what they were ten years ago. This is what scares me, not only as head of a family, but also as the father of children who, thank God, have not become involved in some of these things but have burned off their excess energy through athletics.
I feel that we must reassess the whole situation concerning any changes in this legislation. I hope that when those changes come, we will bear in mind that a young person should not have to carry the burden of his first mistake for the rest of his life. However, we should let that person know what the consequences will be if caught a second time or caught trafficking. I think this is the only way to go. It should be left under the Narcotics Control Act, but the penalty for that first offence must be re-examined. Then, if no further offences occur after a specified period of time, the criminal record should be erased and that person permitted to take his place in the profession of his choice without that cloud or criminal record hanging over his head.
I feel very strongly about this matter. I hope that other responsible hon. members on all sides of this House of Com-
Narcotics
mons and other parents in this chamber will take a very long look at this situation to ensure that we do not develop a society of young people who grow up under the influence of this drug. It affects not only the living, but also the unborn for years to come.
It is with this thought in mind that I say it is of the utmost importance that the House take a long, hard look at any changes taking place here. If necessary, we should perhaps establish a committee to look into the possibility of holding hearings across this country in a selected number of communities to reassess what has happened. We should find out whether the use has been increased. There should be a thorough check and examination of what has been happening through our medical profession and the autopsies which are performed on many accident victims. It is imperative that somewhere along the line we do much more research and obtain more information than that which became available to us through the LeDain Commission. The commission certainly did the very best it could with the information available at that time; but since that time there have been many additional improvements.
